analysis.one_liner: Tightened the legal rules for government surveillance and secret records demands, and cut short the main warrantless foreign-surveillance program.
analysis.headline: Introduced days after the Snowden leaks with 10 Senate cosponsors, the bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have sharply narrowed the government's power to secretly demand phone, financial, and credit records, and would have made the FBI show specific facts before getting such records. It also would have moved up the expiration of the 2008 law that allows broad foreign surveillance — including the program revealed in the 2013 leaks — to June 2015, forcing Congress to vote again on whether to keep it. It added judicial review for gag orders, unclassified public reports on surveillance use, and Inspector General audits.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose phone, email, financial, and credit records could be swept into secret government demands. The bill required specific factual justifications for records requests, cut the time the government could delay telling someone their home was searched, made it easier to challenge gag orders in court, and forced public reporting on how surveillance powers are used. It also shortened the life of the 2008 warrantless-surveillance authority, forcing an open congressional debate on the program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary people's phone and financial records

how_it_helps.text: It moved up the expiration of the FISA Amendments Act's bulk foreign-surveillance authority from 2017 to June 1, 2015, forcing Congress to reconsider those powers rather than letting them run unexamined.

It rolled national security letters — secret FBI demands for phone, bank, and credit records — back to their pre-USA PATRIOT Act scope, and required a written statement of specific facts showing the records are relevant to an investigation.

It gave recipients of secret records demands the right to challenge gag orders in court immediately instead of waiting a year, and ended the legal presumption that disclosure of such an order endangers national security.

It required annual unclassified reports on how surveillance powers are used and their impact on Americans' privacy, plus Inspector General audits of records requests and an Intelligence Community watchdog review of how surveillance data is handled.

analysis.who_pays: The FBI, NSA, and other intelligence agencies, which would lose access to expanded records-gathering tools and face outside audits and public reporting; some investigators argue counterterrorism work would slow.

drawbacks.text: It would have ended the FISA Amendments Act's Section 702 bulk-collection authority more than two years early, eliminating an intelligence tool the government said was needed to track foreign terrorists, with no replacement framework in place.

Rolling national security letters back to their 2001 form would have removed expanded records access that investigators and some judges considered useful in terrorism cases, and shortening delayed-notice search warrants from 30 to 7 days constrains a technique investigators use to avoid tipping off suspects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gains for ordinary people were substantial relative to the modest cost — mainly reduced flexibility and speed for counterterrorism investigators, and the risk of losing bulk collection capability before a replacement is agreed. The bill allowed itself to be debated honestly by forcing an expiration date, which is exactly what made it attractive to civil libertarians and unacceptable to security agencies. Its failure means the pre-Snowden status quo — broad records access, one-year challenge delays, and a 2017 sunset that Congress later extended — continued without the added checks.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Judiciary Committee, where it sat without a markup or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill's entire recorded history is three entries: introduction on June 24, 2013, sponsor remarks, and referral to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.
It never advanced to a committee vote, never reached the Senate floor, and had no House counterpart action in the record.
The 113th Congress ended January 3, 2015, and the bill died with it, having received no vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Intelligence and law enforcement agencies kept their expanded surveillance powers without the added audits, judicial review, and earlier sunset. Telecom and internet providers kept the existing legal framework for complying with secret orders.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Intelligence agencies kept broad surveillance powers

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks in the days after the surveillance disclosures became public.

for.name: Sens. Mike Lee, Mark Udall, Ron Wyden, Richard Blumenthal, Jon Tester
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors of the bill at introduction.

for.name: 10 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill rare bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no markup, no vote, no report — leaving the bill to die at the end of the 113th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but heavily Democratic — 9 Democrats and 1 Republican among 10 cosponsors — and no roll-call vote ever occurred, so the chamber's full position was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill narrowed the government's legal basis for demanding customer records and gave providers explicit rights to challenge gag orders and consult lawyers, but it also wrote detailed, durable nondisclosure procedures into law. Providers would face stricter compliance rules in exchange for clearer rights of their own.

industries.industry: Intelligence and law enforcement agencies (FBI, NSA, DOJ)
industries.note: The bill stripped agencies of expanded records-access authority, shortened a secret search tool, and imposed outside audits and public reporting on classified programs. For ordinary people, this is the surveillance apparatus being constrained, which is the point of the bill.

industries.industry: Consumer reporting agencies and financial institutions
industries.note: Section 627 of the Fair Credit Reporting Act, which let agencies pull credit reports in terrorism investigations, would have been repealed, and banks and credit bureaus would have faced new written-justification and judicial-review rules when the FBI sought their customers' records.
